milestones.title: Milestone 1: Introduction to React and JSX

lessons.title: Lesson 1: React Intro

sections.heading: 1. What is React?
sections.content: React is a front-end JavaScript library. React was developed by the Facebook Software Engineer Jordan Walke. React is also known as React.js or ReactJS. React is a tool for building UI components.

sections.heading: 2. How does React Work?
sections.content: React creates a VIRTUAL DOM in memory. Instead of manipulating the browser's DOM directly, React creates a virtual DOM in memory, where it does all the necessary manipulating, before making the changes in the browser DOM. React only changes what needs to be changed! React finds out what changes have been made, and changes only what needs to be changed.

sections.heading: 3. What You Should Already Know
sections.content: Before you continue you should have a basic understanding of the following: HTML CSS JavaScript Note: The HTML code in this tutorial uses JSX which allows you to write HTML tags inside the JavaScript code. Don't worry if the syntax is unfamiliar, you will learn more about JSX later in this tutorial.

sections.heading: 4. React Environment
sections.content: To use React in production, you need npm which is included with Node.js. Also, you need to set up a React Environment, and choose a build tool. However, you can code directly on FrontEndly through our React live server. Please note that you can only make changes to the code in our live server during the exercise sections.

sections.heading: 5. Modify the React App
sections.content: Let's assume you named your project folder my-react-app. Look inside the my-react-app directory, and you will find a src folder. Inside the src folder, there is a file called App.jsx. This file contains the main React component that you can modify to update the application.

keyTakeaways: React is a JS library for building UI via reusable components.
React uses a Virtual DOM to optimize real DOM updates.
App.jsx in the src folder is the main component to edit.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Rendering HTML in React

sections.heading: 1. The Container
sections.content:
React uses a container to render HTML in a web page. Typically, this container is a
element in the index.html file. You should have a file called index.html in the root directory of your project.

sections.heading: 2. The createRoot Function
sections.content: The createRoot function is located in the main.jsx file in the src folder, and is a built-in function that is used to create a root node for a React application.
sections.code:
import { StrictMode } from 'react'
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client'
import './index.css'
import App from './App.jsx'

createRoot(document.getElementById('root')).render(
<StrictMode>
<App />
</StrictMode>
)

sections.heading: 3. The render Method
sections.content: The render method defines what to render in the HTML container. The result is displayed in the <div id="root"> element.
sections.code:
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client' createRoot(document.getElementById('root')).render(

Welcome!

)

sections.heading: 4. The Root Node
sections.content: The root node is the HTML element where you want to display the result. It is like a container for content, managed by React. It does NOT have to be a <div> element and it does NOT have to have the id='root'. Note: The root node can be called whatever you like.

keyTakeaways: createRoot(element).render(jsx) is how React mounts an app.
The root node element can have any id/tag name, not just <div id='root'>.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Introduction to JSX

sections.heading: 1. What is JSX?
sections.content: JSX stands for JavaScript XML. JSX allows us to write HTML in React. JSX makes it easier to write and add HTML in React.

sections.heading: 2. Coding JSX
sections.content: JSX allows us to write HTML elements in JavaScript and place them in the DOM without any createElement() and/or appendChild() methods. JSX converts HTML tags into react elements. You are not required to use JSX, but JSX makes it easier to write React applications.

sections.heading: 3. Expressions in JSX
sections.content: With JSX you can write expressions inside curly braces { }. The expression can be a React variable, or property, or any other valid JavaScript expression. JSX will execute the expression and return the result.
sections.code:
const myElement =

React is {5 + 5} times better with JSX

;

sections.heading: 4. Elements Must be Closed
sections.content: JSX follows XML rules, and therefore HTML elements must be properly closed. JSX will throw an error if the HTML is not properly closed.

sections.heading: 5. Attribute class = className
sections.content: The class attribute is a much used attribute in HTML, but since JSX is rendered as JavaScript, and the class keyword is a reserved word in JavaScript, you are not allowed to use it in JSX. Use attribute className instead. JSX solved this by using className instead. When JSX is rendered, it translates className attributes into class attributes.

sections.heading: 6. Comments in JSX
sections.content: Comments in JSX are written with {/* */}

sections.heading: 7. JSX in React Components
sections.content: React uses components to build UIs. Components are independent and reusable bits of code. React components are like JavaScript functions, and return HTML. JSX works perfect inside React components

keyTakeaways: JSX = JavaScript XML, syntax extension to write HTML inside JS.
Use className instead of class.
All JSX elements must be properly closed.
Embed JS expressions using { }.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: React JSX Expressions

sections.heading: Expressions
sections.content: One of the most powerful features of JSX is the ability to embed JavaScript expressions directly within your markup. You can insert any valid JavaScript expression inside JSX by wrapping it in curly braces { }. React will evaluate the expression and render the result in the DOM.

sections.heading: Variables
sections.content: Variables are also valid expressions. Insert variables in JSX by wrapping it in curly braces { }.

sections.heading: Function Calls
sections.content: Function calls are valid expressions. Insert function calls in JSX by wrapping it in curly braces { }.

sections.heading: Object Properties
sections.content: Access object properties within JSX:

keyTakeaways: JSX expressions can be literals, variables, function calls, or object properties.
All must be wrapped inside single curly braces { }.

lessons.title: Lesson 1: React JSX Attributes

sections.heading: 1. class = className
sections.content: The class attribute is a much used attribute in HTML, but since JSX is rendered as JavaScript, and the class keyword is a reserved word in JavaScript, you are not allowed to use it in JSX. JSX solved this by using className instead. When JSX is rendered, it translates className attributes into class attributes.

sections.heading: 2. Expressions as Attributes
sections.content: You can also use JavaScript expressions as attribute values. This is very useful for dynamic attributes. Note that the attribute value is not wrapped in quotes, this is important when using expressions (JavaScript variables) as attribute values. If you use quotes, JSX will treat it as a string literals and not a JavaScript expression.

sections.heading: 3. camelCase Event Attributes
sections.content: Event attributes in JSX are written in camelCase.

sections.heading: 4. Boolean Attributes
sections.content: If you pass no value for an attribute, JSX treats it as true. To pass false, you must specify it as an expression.

sections.heading: 5. The style Attribute
sections.content: The style attribute in JSX only accepts a JavaScript object with camelCased CSS property names, rather than a CSS string (as in HTML). The styles are stored in an object. Style properties are written in camelCase, e.g. fontSize, instead of font-size.

keyTakeaways: Use className, camelCase event handlers, and JS-object style attributes.
Expression attribute values are NOT quoted.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Styling React Using CSS

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: There are many ways to style React with CSS, this tutorial will take a closer look at three common ways: Inline styling, CSS stylesheets, CSS Modules.

sections.heading: 1. Inline Styling
sections.content: To style an element with the inline style attribute, the value must be a JavaScript object. Note: In JSX, JavaScript expressions are written inside curly braces, and since JavaScript objects also use curly braces, the styling in the example above is written inside two sets of curly braces {{}}.

sections.heading: 2. camelCased Property Names
sections.content: Since the inline CSS is written in a JavaScript object, properties with hyphen separators, like background-color, must be written with camel case syntax

sections.heading: 3. JavaScript Object
sections.content: You can also create an object with styling information, and refer to it in the style attribute

sections.heading: 4. CSS Stylesheet
sections.content: You can write your CSS styling in a separate file, just save the file with the .css file extension, and import it in your application.

keyTakeaways: Three styling approaches: inline style object, CSS stylesheet import, CSS Modules.
Inline style uses {{ }} with camelCase keys.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: React CSS Modules

sections.heading: 1. What are CSS Modules?
sections.content: CSS Modules let you write CSS that is scoped locally to a specific component. This prevents CSS class name conflicts and makes your styles more maintainable. In React, CSS Modules are CSS files where class names are scoped locally by default. Note: CSS Modules are not a part of the React core library, but are supported by many React build tools. The CSS file have to have the .module.css extension and can be used by importing it into your React file(s).

sections.heading: 3. Using a CSS Module
sections.content: Create a Button component that uses the CSS Module. We import the styles object from the CSS Module. We use styles.mybutton to access the mybutton class. The actual class name of the button will be unique (e.g., _mybutton_q1obu_1).

sections.heading: 4. Composing Classes
sections.content: CSS Modules allow you to combine classes using the composes keyword: Which means that one class can inherit the styles of another class.

sections.heading: 5. Global Classes
sections.content: When using CSS Modules, the classes in the .module.css file can only be used in the component that imports them. This is done by prefixing the class name with a hash of the file name and a unique identifier. However, sometimes you want your classes to be available globally. You can do this with the :global syntax.

sections.heading: 6. Combine Global and Local Classes
sections.content: You can combine global and local classes in the same CSS Module.

keyTakeaways: CSS Modules auto-generate unique class names to avoid conflicts.
Use :global(...) to opt a class out of local scoping.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: React JSX If Statements

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: React supports if statements, but not inside JSX. To be able to use conditional statements in JSX, you should put the if statements outside of the JSX, or you could use a ternary expression instead.

sections.heading: Option 1: Write if statements outside of the JSX code.
sections.content: Write "Banana" if x is less than 10, otherwise "Apple".

sections.heading: Option 2: Use ternary expressions instead.
sections.content: Write "Banana" if x is less than 10, otherwise "Apple".

keyTakeaways: if/else cannot be written directly inside JSX braces.
Use either a precomputed variable, or a ternary operator inline.

lessons.title: Lesson 1: React Components

sections.heading: 1. React Components
sections.content: Components are like functions that return HTML elements. Components are independent and reusable bits of code. They serve the same purpose as JavaScript functions, but work in isolation and return HTML. Components come in two types, Class components and Function components, in this tutorial we will concentrate on Function components. Note: In older React code bases, you may find Class components primarily used. It is now suggested to use Function components along with Hooks. Class components are still supported.

sections.heading: 2. Create Your First Component
sections.content: When creating a React component, the component's name MUST start with an upper case letter. React components returns HTML code.

sections.heading: 3. Rendering a Component
sections.content: To use this component in your application, refer to it like this: <Car />

sections.heading: 4. Props
sections.content: Arguments can be passed into a component as props, which stands for properties. You send the arguments into the component as HTML attributes.

sections.heading: 5. Components in Components
sections.content: We can refer to components inside other components:

sections.heading: 6. Rendering a Component Twice
sections.content: We can render a component multiple times.

sections.heading: 7. Components in Files
sections.content: React is all about re-using code, and it can be a good idea to split your components into separate files. To do that, create a new file in the src folder with a .jsx file extension. Note that the filename must start with an uppercase character.

keyTakeaways: Component names start with an uppercase letter.
Function components return JSX and can be nested/reused.
Split components into separate files using export default.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: React Props

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Props are arguments passed into React components. Props are passed to components via HTML attributes. props stands for properties. React Props are like function arguments in JavaScript and attributes in HTML.

sections.heading: React Props Example
sections.content: Add a brand attribute to the Car element:

sections.heading: Pass Multiple Properties
sections.content: You can send as many properties as you want.

sections.heading: Different Data Types
sections.content: React props can be of any data type, including variables, numbers, strings, objects, arrays, and more. Strings can be sent inside quotes, but numbers, variables, and objects need to be sent inside curly brackets.

sections.heading: Pass Props from Component to Component
sections.content: Attributes are also how you pass data from one component to another, as parameters.

keyTakeaways: Props pass data from parent to child via attribute-like syntax.
Props are read-only and cannot be mutated by the child.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: React Destructuring Props

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: You can limit the properties a component receives by using destructuring. Note: React uses curly brackets to destructure props. This way, the component receives all the properties, but the destructuring makes sure it only uses the ones it needs.

sections.heading: Destructuring ...rest
sections.content: When you don't know how many properties you will receive, you can use the ...rest operator. Meaning: you can specify the properties you need, and the rest will be stored in an object.

sections.heading: Default Values
sections.content: With Destructuring, you can set default values for props. If a property has no value, the default value will be used.

keyTakeaways: Destructure props directly in the function signature: function Car({ brand, model }).
...rest captures unspecified props.
Default values: function Car({ color = "blue" }).

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Hook and React useState

sections.heading: What is a Hook?
sections.content: Hooks are functions that let you "hook into" React state and lifecycle features from functional components. Hooks allow functions to have access to state and other React features without using classes. Note: You must import Hooks from react. State generally refers to application data or properties that need to be tracked.

sections.heading: Hook Rules
sections.content: Hooks can only be called inside React function components. Hooks can only be called at the top level of a component. Hooks cannot be conditional. Note: Hooks will not work in React class components.

sections.heading: React useState Hook
sections.content: The React useState Hook allows us to track state in a function component.

sections.heading: Read State
sections.content: We can now include our state anywhere in our component.

sections.heading: Update State
sections.content: To update our state, we use our state updater function. We should never directly update state. Ex: color = "blue" is not allowed.

sections.heading: What Can State Hold?
sections.content: The useState Hook can be used to keep track of strings, numbers, booleans, arrays, objects, and any combination of these! We could create multiple state Hooks or use one state with an object.

sections.heading: Updating Objects and Arrays in State
sections.content: When the state is updated, the entire state gets overwritten. If we only want to update one property, we use the JavaScript spread operator.

keyTakeaways: useState returns [value, setterFn]; never mutate state directly.
Hooks: top-level only, inside function components only, never conditional.
Use functional updates + spread operator ({ ...prev, key: value }) to update part of an object/array state immutably.
